vignette:
Leilani is a 20-year-old woman from a coastal island community in Oceania. She moved to the mainland two years ago for university and now works as an auditor for a mid-sized firm. She lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment near the office. Her parents and younger brother remain on the island; she calls them every Sunday but has not visited since the stalking began.

Eighteen months ago, a fellow student named Jesse started sitting next to her in the campus library. At first she thought he was just friendly—he smiled, offered gum, commented on her textbooks. She was polite back. Then he began appearing outside her lectures, on the bus she took, at the café where she bought coffee. He knew her schedule. He commented on what she wore, what she ate, who she talked to. She stopped eating in public.

She told him to leave her alone. He said she was being dramatic. The library was a free country. The bus was public transportation. He left notes in her mailbox at the dorm. “You smiled at me first.” “I know you like the ocean.” “I’ll always be close.”

She reported it to campus security. They talked to him. He denied everything. The notes stopped for a week, then began appearing on her phone through anonymous apps. She changed her number. He found it within two days.

Leilani moved out of the dorm and into the apartment she now rents. She told no one her new address except her employer, who needed it for payroll. She filed a police report. The officer was kind but said stalking is hard to prove without a pattern of threats. Jesse had never threatened her outright. He just kept being there.

The semester ended. She transferred to an online program. She stopped going to campus altogether. She thought that would end it. It did not.

Now, Leilani works as an auditor. She sits in a cubicle on the sixth floor, surrounded by spreadsheets and white noise. She is good at her job—meticulous, numerical, able to spot a discrepancy in a column of thousands. But her mind is never fully on the numbers. Every time the elevator dings, she flinches. Every time a coworker stops at her cubicle without warning, her heart hammers so hard she cannot hear their question. She has learned to keep her back to the wall. She always sits facing the door in meetings. She checks the locks on her apartment three times before bed, and once more in the middle of the night.

She no longer goes to the grocery store after dark. She no longer wears headphones in public. She walks home a different route each day, sometimes doubling back to see if anyone follows. She has memorized every exit in her building. She carries pepper spray on her keychain, even though she knows it is likely useless.

The memories come in fragments: the sound of footsteps behind her on the library stairs, the smell of his cheap cologne on a note, the way he smiled when she begged him to stop. She relives the shame of being watched, the helplessness of having nowhere to hide. She wakes up sweating, certain she heard her apartment door unlatch.

Leilani has not dated anyone since the stalking. She deleted all her social media. She cannot stand the feeling of being seen. Even in her office, with forty coworkers around her, she feels exposed. She has stopped eating lunch in the break room. She eats at her desk, facing the door, her chair wedged against the wall.

Her supervisor noticed she seems jumpy. Leilani made an excuse about caffeine. She told her family she is just busy. At night, when the apartment is quiet, she sits on the floor of her closet with her phone in her hand, waiting for a message she knows will never come—and dreading that one day it might.

She still checks the police report status online every morning. Nothing has changed in fourteen months. But she cannot stop checking.
